content: Planned caesarean delivery for women in preterm labor may offer some protective benefits for the baby, but it can also be a traumatic experience for both the mother and the infant. The best mode of delivery for preterm babies, whether they present in a cephalic or breech position, remains a topic of debate. A systematic review was conducted to compare the outcomes of planned immediate caesarean delivery versus planned vaginal delivery for women in preterm labor. The review included six studies involving 122 women, but only four studies with data from 116 women contributed to the analysis. Infant Outcomes: There was no significant difference between planned caesarean delivery and planned vaginal delivery in terms of birth injury to the infant (risk ratio [RR] 0.56, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.05 to 5.62; one trial, 38 women). The only reported birth injuries were a buttock laceration in a baby delivered by caesarean section and mild bruising in a baby delivered vaginally. Birth asphyxia rates were also not significantly different between the two groups (RR 1.63, 95% CI 0.84 to 3.14; one trial, 12 women). Perinatal death rates showed no significant difference between the two delivery methods (RR 0.29, 95% CI 0.07 to 1.14; three trials, 89 women). No data were available regarding neonatal admission to special care or intensive care units. There was no significant difference in Apgar scores of less than seven at five minutes (RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.43 to 1.60; four trials, 115 women). Breastfeeding attempts did not differ significantly between the groups (RR 1.40, 95% CI 0.11 to 17.45; one trial, 12 women). Neonatal seizures or fits were not significantly different between the groups (RR 0.22, 95% CI 0.01 to 4.32; three trials, 77 women). Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy rates were not significantly different (RR 4.00, 95% CI 0.20 to 82.01; one trial, 12 women). Respiratory distress syndrome rates were similar between the groups (RR 0.55, 95% CI 0.27 to 1.10; three trials, 103 women). No data were reported on meconium aspiration. Abnormal childhood follow-up outcomes were not significantly different between the groups (RR 0.65, 95% CI 0.19 to 2.22; one trial, 38 women). Delivery within seven days of study entry showed no significant difference (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.73 to 1.24; two trials, 51 women). Maternal Outcomes: No data were reported on maternal admissions to intensive care units. Seven cases of major maternal postpartum complications occurred in the planned caesarean delivery group, while none were reported in the vaginal delivery group (RR 7.21, 95% CI 1.37 to 38.08; four trials, 116 women). Maternal satisfaction (postnatal) was not reported in the trials. Postpartum hemorrhage rates showed no significant difference between the groups. Maternal puerperal pyrexia (fever after childbirth) was significantly more common in the caesarean delivery group (RR 2.98, 95% CI 1.18 to 7.53; three trials, 89 women). Other maternal infections were also more frequent in the caesarean delivery group (RR 2.63, 95% CI 1.02 to 6.78; three trials, 103 women). Wound infection rates were not significantly different (RR 1.16, 95% CI 0.18 to 7.70; three trials, 103 women). Maternal hospital stays longer than 10 days were not significantly different between the groups (RR 1.27, 95% CI 0.35 to 4.65; three trials, 78 women). The need for blood transfusion was not estimable due to insufficient data. Conclusions: There is insufficient evidence to determine the benefits or risks of a policy of planned immediate caesarean delivery for preterm babies. Further research is needed in this area, but recruitment for such studies has proven to be challenging.
